address_cn: 桂林市阳朔县遇龙河景区(近朝阳码头)
hook: Drift on a handmade bamboo raft through China's most intimate karst landscape — crystal-clear water, ancient stone bridges, and rice paddies framed by towering limestone peaks, all without a motor in sight.
honest_description: The Yulong River is the Li River's quieter, prettier little sister — a gentle tributary where hand-poled bamboo rafts glide past karst peaks, century-old stone bridges, and rural villages with zero motorized boats allowed. Unlike the Li River's large tourist cruise ships, here it's just you, your raft operator, and the landscape. The most popular route (Jinlong Bridge to Jiuxian) takes about 90 minutes through 9 small dam drops that add mild excitement. The scenery is genuinely breathtaking — emerald water so clear you see fish below, peaks rising straight from rice paddies, and a pastoral atmosphere that feels untouched by modernity. Peak season queues can be brutal (1-2 hour waits), tickets sell out fast, and prices are steep for what's essentially floating on bamboo, but almost every reviewer says it's worth it. Best combined with cycling along the river for the ultimate Yangshuo experience.

foreigner_top_questions.question: How do I book tickets as a foreigner?
foreigner_top_questions.answer: You need a passport or ID to purchase tickets. Buy through Trip.com or at the dock ticket office. Tickets typically go on sale at 8:00 PM the night before via the official WeChat mini-program, but foreigners may find Trip.com easier. During peak season (holidays, summer), tickets sell out within minutes. Arrive at the dock by 7:30 AM for same-day purchases. Each raft fits 2 people and is priced per raft (¥200-320 depending on route), not per person. If you're having trouble securing tickets — especially during holidays — message our concierge team and we can book through the Chinese-language system on your behalf.

foreigner_top_questions.question: Which route should I choose?
foreigner_top_questions.answer: Jinlong Bridge to Jiuxian (金龙桥-旧县) is the most recommended route — 6km, about 90 minutes, with 9 dam drops and the best scenery including three famous ancient bridges. Shuiedi to Gongnong Bridge (水厄底-工农桥) is shorter (40-50 min, 3km) and cheaper if you're short on time. The longer route is worth the extra cost and time.

experience_format_note: Activity-based experience. You board a 2-person bamboo raft at a dock and are poled downstream by a raft operator. No paddling required from you. You sit on bamboo chairs on the raft. The raft goes over small dam drops (0.5-1m) that create mild splashing — lift your feet and hold on. Life jackets are mandatory. Bring a phone waterproof bag.
vibe: Serene and pastoral — like floating through a living Chinese landscape painting, punctuated by the gentle excitement of small rapids.

time_needed.quick_visit: 40-50 minutes (Shuiedi to Gongnong Bridge short route)
time_needed.recommended: 1.5-2 hours (Jinlong Bridge to Jiuxian full route — the best experience)
time_needed.deep_dive: Half day (rafting plus cycling the riverside path back, stopping at cafes and viewpoints)

best_time.best_time_of_day: Early morning (first departure around 8:00 AM) for the most peaceful experience, misty atmosphere, and smallest crowds. Late afternoon (4:00-5:00 PM) for golden hour light on the peaks, but you'll be rushed to finish before closing.
best_time.worst_time: Major holidays (National Day, May Day, Chinese New Year, July-August summer holidays) — expect 1-2 hour queues and rafts packed nose-to-tail on the river. The magic disappears when you're in a traffic jam of bamboo rafts.
best_time.seasonal_notes: April-October is rafting season (high water). April-May and September-October offer the best balance of water levels, pleasant weather, and manageable crowds. July-August is hottest with the most tourists. Winter (November-March) has lower water levels — rafts may scrape bottom and the ride is less smooth.
best_time.pro_tip: Book the Jinlong Bridge to Jiuxian route and go on a weekday. After the raft ride, rent an e-bike at Jiuxian and cycle the Ten-Mile Gallery (十里画廊) riverside path back — this combination is the quintessential Yangshuo experience.

getting_in.price_rmb: ¥200-320 per raft (2 people) depending on route. Single riders pay the full raft price.

price_breakdown.highlight: Shorter scenic route, good for limited time
The classic route — 9 dam drops, 3 ancient bridges, best scenery. Most recommended.

getting_in.booking_required: Strongly recommended during peak season. Tickets often sell out on holidays and weekends. Book the night before via Trip.com or the official WeChat mini-program (tickets release at 8:00 PM). Same-day purchase possible on weekdays.
getting_in.booking_method: Trip.com (easiest for foreigners), or purchase at dock ticket offices. Note: some reviewers report Trip.com prices being higher than dock prices — check both. Passport required for ticket purchase.
getting_in.passport_accepted: Yes — bring your physical passport. Required for ticket purchase and boarding registration.
getting_in.what_to_bring: Passport (mandatory). Waterproof phone bag (essential — you will get splashed). Sandals or water shoes. Spare dry clothes in a bag. Sunscreen and hat. Camera in waterproof case. Small cash for tipping the raft operator (optional but appreciated).
getting_in.queue_situation: Weekdays: minimal wait. Weekends: 30-60 minutes. Major holidays: 1-2+ hours. Rafts are numbered and called in sequence — there's a waiting hall with seating. Check the official WeChat mini-program for real-time queue status.
getting_in.language_barrier_rating: mandarin-only — Raft operators speak only Chinese. Ticket staff may have very basic English. The experience is visual and doesn't require language — just sit, enjoy, and hold on during the dam drops.

highlights.name: Dam Drops (堰坝)
highlights.description: The Jinlong-Jiuxian route features 9 small dams where the raft drops 0.5-1 meter, creating a gentle splash of excitement. The largest drops feel like a mini water ride — hold your feet up and grip the bamboo chair. Photographers on the banks capture your reaction (photos available for ¥20).
highlights.foreigner_note: Not actually dangerous — life jackets are mandatory and the drops are small. But the splash of cool river water combined with the adrenaline makes these the most memorable moments of the ride.
highlights.tip: Lift your feet high during drops to keep shoes dry. Hold your phone in a waterproof bag. The photo point at the main dam is actually worth buying (¥20) — they capture a great action shot.

highlights.name: Ancient Stone Bridges
highlights.description: The Jinlong-Jiuxian route passes three remarkable bridges: Jinlong Bridge (Ming Dynasty), Yulong Bridge (oldest, also Ming Dynasty, 60m long), and Xiangui Bridge (Song Dynasty, built 1123 AD — the oldest stone arch bridge in Guangxi, so low it nearly touches the water).
highlights.foreigner_note: Xiangui Bridge dates to 1123 AD — nearly 900 years old, and you float right under it. The bridge is so low your raft barely clears it, creating a dramatic passage.
highlights.tip: Duck your head when passing under Xiangui Bridge — it's very close to the water surface. Have your camera ready for the approach shot.

highlights.name: Karst Peak and Rice Paddy Scenery
highlights.description: The entire route is framed by towering limestone karst peaks rising directly from flat rice paddies and the river. The combination of emerald water, green peaks, and pastoral farmland creates the quintessential Guilin landscape experience — more intimate and photogenic than the larger Li River cruise.
highlights.foreigner_note: This is the scenery that made Guilin/Yangshuo world-famous. The Yulong River is less commercialized than the Li River, offering a more authentic and intimate experience of the same landscape.
highlights.tip: Bring a zoom lens for the peaks and a wide angle for the panoramas. The raft operator will pause at scenic points if you ask — tip a little and they're happy to slow down.

what_visitors_miss.what: Fuli Bridge (富里桥) at the river's source
what_visitors_miss.why: A beautiful old bridge near the headwaters of the Yulong River — a quiet, photogenic spot that most tourists skip because it's not on the main rafting routes. Worth a motorbike detour (¥15 from locals) before your raft trip.

what_visitors_miss.what: Cycling the riverside path after rafting
what_visitors_miss.why: Most visitors take a car back after rafting and miss the best part — the riverside cycling path from Jiuxian through the Ten-Mile Gallery is equally stunning and lets you stop at viewpoints, cafes, and villages at your own pace.
The Yulong River in early morning mist is ethereal — wisps of fog floating between karst peaks, fishermen casting nets. Most tourists don't arrive until mid-morning and miss this magical hour.

strategy.smart_route: Book the Jinlong Bridge to Jiuxian route for the next morning → Arrive at Jinlong Bridge dock by 7:30-8:00 AM → Enjoy the 90-minute raft ride → At Jiuxian dock, rent an e-bike (¥50-80/day) → Cycle south along the river through the Ten-Mile Gallery → Stop at the 'Murakami Coffee' (村上春树咖啡馆) for photos → Continue cycling back to Yangshuo town → Evening in West Street.
strategy.what_to_skip: The very short routes (30-minute options) feel too rushed and don't include the best dam drops. The Li River cruise, while grand, doesn't offer the same intimate bamboo raft experience — do both if you have time, but if you must choose one, the Yulong River is more unique.
strategy.pro_tips: Wear sandals you don't mind getting wet. Bring a dry bag for your phone, wallet, and camera. Raft operators appreciate small tips (¥10-20) and will point out scenic highlights and slow down for photos if you're friendly. The raft has a small umbrella for sun/rain protection. If traveling solo, you'll still need to pay for the full 2-person raft — try to find another solo traveler at the dock to split the cost.

heads_up.warning: You WILL get splashed during dam drops
heads_up.advice: Wear quick-dry clothing and water shoes/sandals. Put everything valuable in a waterproof bag. Lift your feet during dam drops — water splashes up from below. Your bottom half may get wet.

heads_up.warning: Tickets sell out fast during peak season
heads_up.advice: During holidays and summer weekends, tickets sell out within minutes of release. Book the night before at 8:00 PM via Trip.com or the official mini-program. If sold out, try showing up at the dock early — cancellations sometimes free up spots. Our concierge team can also monitor availability and book through the Chinese mini-program, which often has slots that don't appear on Trip.com.
Children under 1 meter tall, pregnant women, elderly over 70, and people with heart conditions are NOT allowed on the rafts. Life jackets are mandatory. These rules are enforced.
Combined passenger weight should not exceed 160kg per 2-person raft. If exceeded, you'll need to buy a second raft. This is not mentioned on all booking platforms — check in advance.

foreigners_watch_out: Passport is required for ticket purchase AND boarding — bring your physical passport, not a copy.

Third-party booking platforms (including Trip.com) sometimes charge significantly more than the dock ticket office. One reviewer paid ¥452 on Trip.com for a ¥320 route. Check dock prices first if possible.

Raft operators speak only Chinese. Communication is minimal anyway — they know the route. A smile and a '谢谢' (xièxie) goes a long way. If you need to communicate something specific to your raft operator, drop us a message and we can translate or even call them on your behalf.
The photography service at dam drops (¥20/photo) is decent quality and a fun souvenir. They'll also send a digital copy via QR code scan.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: Tickets sold out for your desired route
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: Try an alternative route — less popular docks like Fuli Bridge or Yulong Bridge often have availability when Jinlong Bridge is sold out. The scenery is similar throughout.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: Rent an e-bike and cycle the riverside path instead. The views are equally stunning and you have more freedom to stop and explore. Stand-up paddleboarding (SUP) is also available at some points along the river.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: River water level too low for rafting
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: During dry winter months, some routes may be suspended. Check with the dock or your hotel before heading out. The Shuiedi to Gongnong Bridge route tends to have enough water year-round.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: Cycle the riverside path — arguably even better in winter when the crowds are gone and the air is crisp.

if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: Most docks have small shops selling waterproof bags (¥10-20). If your phone got wet, turn it off immediately and dry it. Replacement clothing available at shops near the docks.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: This is why preparation matters — always bring a waterproof phone bag and dry change of clothes.

preparation.what_to_wear: Quick-dry shorts and T-shirt. Water sandals or shoes you don't mind getting wet. A hat for sun protection. Light rain jacket if weather is uncertain.
preparation.what_to_bring: Passport (mandatory). Waterproof phone bag (essential). Sunscreen. Water bottle. Dry change of clothes in a bag. Small cash for tips and photo purchases. Camera in waterproof housing if you have one.
preparation.what_not_to_bring: Nice shoes (they will get wet). Heavy bags (no storage on the raft). Valuables you can't waterproof.

physical_accessibility.physical_details: You sit on the raft — no physical exertion required. The raft operator does all the work. Getting on and off the raft requires stepping onto wet bamboo (slightly slippery). Dam drops create mild jolts but nothing strenuous.
physical_accessibility.age_notes: Children must be over 1 meter tall. Elderly over 70 are not permitted. Otherwise suitable for all ages who can sit comfortably for 45-90 minutes.
physical_accessibility.health_warnings: People with heart conditions, high blood pressure, or pregnant women are prohibited from rafting. Sun exposure is constant — wear sunscreen and a hat. Motion sickness is rare but possible on longer routes.

concierge_opportunities.action: Book Yulong River bamboo rafting tickets
concierge_opportunities.value_to_user: Guarantees a spot during peak season when tickets sell out fast. English-language booking process is much easier than the Chinese-only official mini-program. We can also book directly through the Chinese system at dock prices — message us the night before and we'll secure your slot as soon as tickets release at 8 PM.

concierge_opportunities.action: Book a Yangshuo day package (rafting + cycling + Ten-Mile Gallery)
concierge_opportunities.value_to_user: Combines the three best Yangshuo activities into one organized day with transport, avoiding the logistics of arranging each separately.

useful_chinese.english: Slow down a bit (ask the raft operator for photos)

pair_with.suggestion: Ten-Mile Gallery Cycling (十里画廊骑行)
pair_with.why: The natural continuation after rafting — rent an e-bike at the end dock and cycle the riverside path through karst peaks and rice paddies back to Yangshuo. The perfect complement to the water experience.
pair_with.travel_time: Starts at the raft end dock

pair_with.why: After a morning of rafting and cycling, West Street offers evening food, drinks, and nightlife. The contrast between pastoral river and buzzing tourist street captures the full Yangshuo experience.

pair_with.suggestion: Impression Liu Sanjie Show (印象刘三姐)
pair_with.why: An outdoor night spectacle directed by Zhang Yimou using the Li River as a stage with 600 performers. The perfect evening activity after a day on the Yulong River.

cultural_context: The Yulong River (meaning 'Dragon Encounter River') has been a lifeline for farming communities in the Yangshuo region for centuries. The ancient stone bridges that span it — some dating to the Song Dynasty (1123 AD) — were built to connect villages separated by the river and remain in use today. Bamboo rafting here started organically in 2001 when a local fisherman took a photographer out on his fishing raft for better photo angles. Today, over 300 raft operators work the river, all from local villages, using the same hand-poling technique their ancestors used for fishing. The prohibition on motorized boats is deliberate — the river is protected as a natural heritage site, preserving both the ecology and the timeless atmosphere that makes it special.

photo_spots.location: Approaching Yulong Bridge from the raft
photo_spots.tip: The ancient bridge framed by karst peaks behind it is the classic Yulong River composition. Shoot from the raft as you approach — the bridge reflection in still water is stunning.
photo_spots.why: A 600-year-old stone bridge with karst mountains behind — the definitive image of the Yulong River.

photo_spots.location: Dam drop action shots (taken by on-site photographers)
photo_spots.tip: The photographers positioned at the main dam capture great action shots for ¥20. They also send a digital QR code version. Worth buying.
photo_spots.why: A fun, dynamic photo you can't take yourself while gripping the raft.

photo_spots.tip: After rafting, cycle the path and stop at the elevated viewpoints — several offer sweeping river-and-peak panoramas.
photo_spots.why: The aerial perspective from the cycling path shows the river winding through karst peaks in a way you can't see from the raft itself.

card_hook: Bamboo, clear water, karst peaks — China's most serene river ride.
